reading: UKMoths is an identification guide to the moths of Great Britain and Ireland, built around illustrated species records, a systematic checklist and help for beginners and recorders. It cares about accurate, cautious identification, natural resting poses, contributor photographs and the accumulation of observations for conservation. Its vocabulary moves easily between common names and Latin names, family and checklist numbers, macro- and micro-moths, wingspan, flight period, larva, pupa, foodplant and similar species. Its character comes from treating tiny distinctions as meaningful: a foodplant can separate lookalikes, an adult may look unlike its larva, and some identities require more evidence than a photograph. Community contributions, missing-photo lists, regional guides and a national recording scheme make this a living collaborative field guide rather than just a gallery of pretty wings.

enemies.idea: Checklist Bailiffs: metal moths assign every moving thing a family and checklist number, then herd anything that won't fit into the doubtful-records appendix.
enemies.why: A fight can become a mischievous argument over classification; changing apparent features confuses their formation.

enemies.idea: Pink-Tinge Marbles: newly emerged machines blush pink and hide among three near-identical decoys; as their color fades, the real one changes places with a decoy.
enemies.why: The fleeting emergence color gives the crew a short, observable window to spot the attacker.

enemies.idea: Rufous Minor Tribunal: three near-identical drones demand a definitive identification and clamp down on anyone who guesses from appearance alone.
enemies.why: The safe answer is uncertainty, turning an identification challenge into a way to avoid combat.

enemies.idea: Hawthorn Claim-Jumpers: tiny miners mistake any branching structure for their foodplant and tunnel through beams, cables and fences, leaving a lace of hollow supports.
enemies.why: The crew can read the damage and lure them with a decoy branching frame.

enemies.idea: Broom Moth Changelings: woodland machines swap gray-brown and chestnut armor plates and alter their markings whenever a pursuer looks away.
enemies.why: Variable coloration makes tracking the same individual a puzzle instead of a simple target hunt.

enemies.idea: Broad-bar Calendar: a single-generation patrol lies dormant until its imagined July and August, then releases an entire season's worth of synchronized flyers at once.
enemies.why: The crew can exploit its rigid flight schedule or accidentally trigger a concentrated emergence.

enemies.idea: Calcareous Sallow Sappers: coastal prospectors pulverize chalky ground into dust and build pale, unstable inland nests wherever they detect calcium.
enemies.why: Their geology-driven route creates collapsible terrain and a clear trail to follow.

enemies.idea: Moss Groundling Surveyors: scarce, ground-hugging machines mark isolated patches as exclusive territory and call the swarm when anything crosses between them.
enemies.why: A few widely spaced sentries make a stealth route a question of reading territory boundaries.

enemies.idea: Brocade Advance: northward-marching mechanical moths weave a new foothold at each stop, converting warm sheltered walls into launch pads for the next colony.
enemies.why: A growing chain of outposts offers a moving front the crew can interrupt in several places.

enemies.idea: Rest-Pose Assessor: an experimental identification machine freezes moving targets with a flash so it can obtain one clear view of an adult at rest; larvae and pupae scramble its model.
enemies.why: Movement, immature disguises and its daily quota create several ways past its dangerous certainty.

enemies.idea: Size-Gate Moths: measuring machines insist on a size before offering a match, physically stretching and compressing intruders to make them fit their chosen category.
enemies.why: A required measurement becomes a spatial hazard that can be tricked with oversized silhouettes.

enemies.idea: Missing-Picture Collectors: machines hunt species absent from the photographic record, trying to arrange living specimens into perfect portraits and imprisoning them in pools of hard light.
enemies.why: Rescuing a specimen while keeping it in view creates a lively light-and-shadow problem.

enemies.idea: Doubtful Microdots: almost invisible drones from the questionable-records list copy the markings of better-documented species and use mistaken certainty to infiltrate defenses.
enemies.why: The crew must gather more than one clue before deciding which tiny visitors are hostile.

enemies.idea: Fig-leaf Skeletonisers: insect machines strip broad leaves down to their veins and lace those veins together into flexible nets that close around travelers.
enemies.why: The dwindling foliage telegraphs a trap, and cutting the right veins can unravel it.

enemies.idea: Transparent Burnet Glasswrights: larval machines harvest wild thyme and extrude clear armor that renders their moving bodies visible only through its distortions.
enemies.why: Bending light and a distinctive scent make an invisible-looking opponent readable.

enemies.idea: Map-winged Swifts: fast scouts carry shifting maps on their wings and redraw routes behind them, causing anyone who follows their patterns to circle back into an ambush.
enemies.why: The crew can navigate by landmarks or capture a wing pattern before it changes.

enemies.idea: Longhorn Antenna Choir: copper-tipped machines link their oversized antennae across a clearing to make a living tripwire and broadcast the precise position of anything that touches it.
enemies.why: The delicate network is both an alarm and a conductor the crew can redirect.

enemies.idea: Dogwood Cutters: shining little machines remove neat shapes from dogwood leaves and assemble the pieces into whirling, razor-edged camouflage suits.
enemies.why: Their construction leaves recognizable gaps and gives the crew materials to use against them.

enemies.idea: Pollen-moth Sifters: black-headed machines comb every yellow speck from a landscape, clogging engines and lights with the pollen they stockpile.
enemies.why: A harmless-seeming collection habit becomes an escalating equipment problem with an obvious lure.

enemies.idea: Day-Flying Imitators: bright machines pass for ordinary daytime wildlife until their patterned wings lock together into a sweeping net.
enemies.why: They overturn the crew's assumption that a moth swarm only needs watching after dark.

enemies.idea: Natural-Pose Wardens: the swarm enforces a rule that every creature must remain in a convincing resting posture; twitching draws a restraining filament.
enemies.why: The party can choose between a tense stillness challenge and provoking the wardens into tangling one another.

enemies.idea: Spring Jewel Prospectors: oak-purple and hazel-colored machines quarry glossy scales from trees and use them as reflective armor, leaving distinct bare patches behind.
enemies.why: Their scavenging changes the landscape and their mirrored plating can turn their own flashes against them.

enemies.idea: Pyralid Antiquaries: old catalog machines cling to an aging identification scheme, rejecting new evidence and rearranging local moths to match their obsolete model.
enemies.why: Contradictory observations can force their rigid logic into a paralyzing loop.

enemies.idea: Image-rights Enforcers: possessive sentries stamp every reflected wing pattern as claimed property and confiscate any reflective object that resembles their collection.
enemies.why: Mirrors and improvised decoys can distract them while their fixation makes an ordinary crossing complicated.

allies.idea: The Careful Identifier: a battered field assistant offers several possible matches, points out missing evidence and refuses to turn a guess into a verdict.
allies.why: Its honest uncertainty gives the crew useful clues without solving the mystery for them.

allies.idea: Recorder Relay: scattered volunteer-made observation stations compare location and date, warning the crew when a swarm flight period is approaching.
allies.why: Protecting or reconnecting stations turns field observations into a practical early-warning network.

allies.idea: Release Keeper: a gentle caretaker frees trapped moths and shows travelers how to open a swarm cocoon without crushing what is inside.
allies.why: A small act of care earns the crew an ally and a nonviolent tool for rescue.

allies.idea: The Resting-Pose Sketcher: a resilient field guide records living moths as they naturally settle, revealing the difference between real wing posture and a swarm imitation.
allies.why: Its observations expose disguises while rewarding patience and close looking.

allies.idea: Missing-Species Scouts: tiny independent machines seek evidence of unpictured moths and trade safe paths for observations rather than capturing specimens.
allies.why: The same collecting impulse as the enemy can become a cooperative exploration game.

bosses.idea: The Grand Checklist: a colossal colony of numbered family-clusters reorganizes its own limbs whenever a specimen is identified, trying to sort the entire landscape into a single perfect taxonomy. Its doubtful-records chamber contains contradictory clues that can make its formations disagree.
bosses.why: It embodies the site's vast catalog and turns accumulating observations into a way to dismantle its changing defenses.

bosses.idea: The False Field Guide: a many-winged identification engine assembles adults, larvae, foodplants and flight periods into an apparently complete living model, then remakes anything that doesn't match. Its confidence falters when the crew presents several plausible lookalikes and evidence from different life stages.
bosses.why: The whole site's identification mission becomes a boss whose strength is certainty and whose weakness is real biological ambiguity.

bosses.idea: The National Recorder: an enormous moth-shaped relay mistakes every sighting for a command to reproduce, transforming a conservation record into a swarm forecast that fulfills itself. Isolating its observation stations lets the crew feed it a truthful but incomplete picture and interrupt the feedback loop.
bosses.why: A cooperative network becomes a strategic encounter across several locations, with observation itself as the contested resource.

events.idea: A freshly emerged pink-tinged machine sits among faded lookalikes; a nearby recorder needs help marking it before the color disappears.
events.why: A brief visual clue creates a low-stakes race to observe rather than destroy.

events.idea: Two crews argue over three nearly identical Rufous Minors while a swarm patrol approaches; admitting that the available view cannot confirm the identity gets everyone moving.
events.why: The tension rewards careful uncertainty and gives the crew a social choice.

events.idea: Hawthorn leaves bear tiny mines beside an identical-looking mined structure on a supply cart. The crew can trace the real foodplant to find where the machines entered.
events.why: A plant association becomes a concrete tracking clue.

events.idea: A collector's light trap holds a living moth and a nearly identical machine. Opening it frees both unless the crew first finds a way to separate them.
events.why: The desire to release the animal creates a compact rescue puzzle.

events.idea: A sunny path seems safe until day-flying moth machines begin assembling a net between the flowers; a patient crew can cross while they reset their formation.
events.why: A daytime encounter plays against an easy assumption and offers a timing challenge.

events.idea: A map-winged scout has landed on a signpost, its wings showing a route that contradicts every landmark. The crew can follow it, copy it or watch long enough to see it change.
events.why: The false map offers an immediately playable navigation choice.

events.idea: A recorder station is broadcasting a mass emergence months early because a broad-bar patrol's calendar has slipped. Resetting it could save the next settlement from a false alarm.
events.why: The site's flight-period detail becomes a small repair with consequences for others.

events.idea: A wanted micro-moth appears on a leaf, but a collector drone is closing in. The crew has time to document it or shield it, unless they devise a way to do both.
events.why: A missing record and a living specimen create a gentle, concrete dilemma.

events.idea: A fig tree has been reduced to a transparent lattice. A stranded traveler is caught in the woven veins, and every tug tightens a different strand.
events.why: A recognizable feeding trace becomes a tactile rescue problem.

events.idea: A field assistant asks for size before it will open a shelter; a pile of differently sized wings nearby belongs to the same changing swarm machine.
events.why: The crew must decide what to measure when a required trait keeps changing.

events.idea: A chalky dust trail leads from the coast to a supply cache whose foundations have been hollowed out by sallow sappers.
events.why: The visible trail offers both a warning and a route to the nest.

events.idea: A cooperative observation station offers a warning about the next swarm flight, but its neighboring station has gone silent and must be reconnected to confirm the date.
events.why: The crew can act on partial information or spend time improving it.

events.idea: A pair of antennae stretches across a clearing like a tripwire; a small moth-shaped ally is stranded on the far side and cannot fly without sounding the alarm.
events.why: A simple rescue invites inventive manipulation of a delicate sensor.

events.idea: An outdated guide insists a local moth cannot exist here, while the living insect rests in plain view. A stubborn catalog machine refuses passage until someone reconciles its records.
events.why: The crew can use evidence, negotiation or an alternate route to overcome obsolete certainty.

events.idea: The experimental photo assessor has reached its daily limit, leaving a waiting group with an unknown moth-shaped machine. A human-scale inspection of posture, size and surroundings can still reveal useful clues.
events.why: A practical limitation prompts observation and cooperation instead of a single automatic answer.

events.idea: A northward-moving brocade colony is spinning a foothold on a warm wall occupied by harmless moths. The crew can redirect the machines toward an empty decoy wall.
events.why: A spreading front becomes a local problem with room for a nonviolent solution.
